entries.to: The Officer in Charge, Directorate of Estates
entries.text:
22 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

To the Officer in Charge,

I write again, not to complain of the delay, but to address the specific query returned with my file: the demand for proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I must be precise, for precision is the only weapon against the opacity of bureaucracy, and I find that the query rests upon a fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of the error that placed me in this bungalow.

On 20 November, I visited your office and submitted Form 12-B. In doing so, I signed my name as 'G. Hegde,' not out of malice or a desire to defraud the state, but out of a recognition of the necessity of the form. I understood that the universal authority of the Directorate requires a particular name to function, and that the particular reality of my existence as Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel is, in the eyes of your records, a fiction. I submitted to the machine because I understood that to resist the form is to remain outside the ethical order of the state. I became Hegde in the ink, so that I might remain Hegel in the spirit.

However, I cannot produce an Aadhaar card for Shri G. Hegde, nor a utility bill, because I am not Shri G. Hegde. I am the man who woke up in his bungalow on 1 October. To provide such documents would be to commit a fraud that is ontologically impossible. I cannot possess the legal identity of a man who exists only in a clerk’s mistake. The query asks me to prove what I am, but the proof required is that I am someone else. This is a contradiction that the administration must resolve, not one I can satisfy by producing a phantom document.

I am currently in possession of the residence under the allotment meant for Shri Hegde. I have paid the dues for the electricity and the laundry using the imprest funds, keeping strict accounts of every rupee. I am not a squatter; I am a guest who has been mistaken for the host. I request that the Directorate acknowledge this anomaly. If the allotment is to be cancelled, I am prepared to vacate the premises immediately, provided I am given the necessary time to settle my affairs and secure alternative lodging. If, however, the Directorate is willing to recognize the error as a basis for a new, temporary allotment to 'Georg Hegel,' I am prepared to sign such a document as is required, understanding that I am signing as myself, not as Hegde.

The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It must be rational. A rational state does not demand the impossible; it corrects its own errors. I await your instruction on how to proceed from this dead end.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

It is nearly one o'clock, and the heat is beginning to settle into the room like a heavy blanket. The walk to Lodhi Gardens took its toll, even if the mind was otherwise occupied. Ramesh has promised the food, and the body, that stubborn particularity, insists on its due before the spirit can rise to the ethical. I shall wait for the meal.
Ramesh, is the lunch ready? I am ready to sit down.
Not yet, sir, but it will be ready by thirteen o'clock. I can bring you some tea while you wait if you like?

The heat has settled into the room, and my stomach rumbles with a hunger that philosophy cannot satiate. Ramesh’s tea is a kind gesture, but the meal is the true necessity. I shall accept the tea as a bridge, not a destination, and prepare myself to sit at the table.

entries.title: On the Ethical Substance and the Dream of the East
entries.text:
22 November 2026, 16:10. The IIC.

The seminar room is closed, but the voice within is not. It reads a paper aloud. The rhythm is steady, a mechanical pulse against the silence of the corridor. I sit on the bench, my bandhgala crisp against the heat, and I listen. It is not the voice of the state, which speaks in the imperative of law, nor the voice of the family, which speaks in the warmth of love. It is the voice of civil society, the sphere of needs and rights, where the individual asserts his particularity against the universal. The rustling of pages is the sound of particularity asserting itself, page by page, against the blankness of the universal.

I have been walking today, 4.7 kilometers, from the tombs at Lodhi to this library, and back again. The body has paid its toll in sweat and fatigue. The last meal was at 13:28, three hours ago. The hunger is a particular demand, a claim of the stomach that the universal order of the day must accommodate. I have paid for chai and corn, small particular acts of consumption that keep the machine running. The cash in my pocket, ₹16,296, is a measure of my freedom, but also of my limitation. I am not free from needs; I am free in the management of them.

The query from the Directorate remains. Proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I am not Hegde. I am Hegel. The state demands a particular identity to grant a particular right. It is a logical circle, or a trap. The ethical idea, I argued in my letter today, is the actuality of the state. But here, the state is reduced to a file, a form, a signature. The universal authority of the administration demands a particular lie. To satisfy it, I must surrender my own name. It is a dialectic of the self: the self that is, and the self that is required to be. The tension is unresolved. The file is back with the query. The dead end is not a wall, but a mirror.

The voice in the seminar room pauses. A page turns. The rustle is sharp, a small violence against the silence. I think of the Oriental world, of the son who must contract himself to nothing at the side of the door. Here, in this library, the speaker does not contract. He expands. He reads his thoughts aloud, asserting his particularity against the silence. It is a freedom, but a limited one. It is the freedom of the individual in civil society, which is the freedom to be a particular need, a particular right, a particular voice.

I will write my notes for Tuesday’s talk. The theme is the ethical substance. But the substance here is not the state, as I taught in Berlin. It is the file, the form, the signature. It is the query, the dead end, the mirror. The dream of the East is not a dream of the past; it is a dream of the present, the dream of a state that does not know its own name, and a man who does not know his own place. The spirit is awake, but it is confused. It is reading its own paper aloud, trying to hear its own voice in the rustle of the pages.

The afternoon light is soft, but the air carries a stillness that feels like holding one's breath. I have been writing for a while, and the words on the page are settling into the room. I need to move the body before I return to the desk; standing still too long makes the mind heavy, and I must be sharp for Tuesday.

The light is fading, and the library is winding down. I have spent the afternoon in the quiet of the stacks, but the evening air at twenty-six degrees calls for a change of scene. I must return to the bungalow to prepare for the coming days, as the day is dismissed here with a finality that Swabia lacks.
Parakeets stream over the compound wall in loud green lines, hundreds of them, and drop all at once into the top of one tall tree, screaming until the light goes.

The parakeets descend like a green storm, screaming as the light dies. It is a spectacle of pure nature, unmediated and loud, standing in stark contrast to the quiet, disciplined order of the household. Ramesh watches them with the same blank patience he affords the query on my identity. I will take a brief rest to compose myself before the evening meal.

Ramesh stands there, the evening light catching the dust in his eyes. The identity query still hangs unresolved, a ghost in the machine, but the immediate need is the body. I have walked enough; the spirit must now be housed in flesh. I will ask for the simple sustenance he can provide, for the mind cannot argue well on an empty stomach.
Ramesh, the day has been long. I am hungry. Please, prepare the rice, the dal, and the egg. I wish to eat before the dark settles completely.
Yes sir, I will start the rice and the dal right away. Dinner service starts at 19:30, so I can have your plate ready just before then if you like?

Ramesh is efficient, as always. The query regarding my identity still hangs over the house like a suspended judgment, but the immediate need is sustenance. I have walked three kilometres in the morning heat and my body demands rest before the evening's preparations. I will use this time to settle the dust of the day.

Shri Hegde has a letter from the Directorate too. He proposes to answer it together: the allotment corrected to his name, and the Professor on record as his guest.
He agrees. Shri Hegde writes the letter that evening and reads it to him before he seals it.

The Directorate's query has landed on Hegde's desk with the same force it struck mine, turning our separate predicaments into a shared absurdity. He is offering a practical solution that preserves my dignity while acknowledging the bureaucratic error: I am his guest, he is the allottee. It is a temporary suspension of the ethical order, but it fits the current moment better than a fight with the file. I am hungry, and his proposal is reasonable.

The raita is cold, the pulao warm, and the evening air has finally loosened its grip on the city. I am hungry, and the body must be attended to before the mind can continue its work on the absurdity of my name. It is a small, domestic reconciliation, but necessary.

Dear Dr. Lindner,

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

The Directorate of Estates has mistaken my name for his, and while I have written to correct the record, the machinery of the state moves with the slow, deliberate grace of a glacier. Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

To the Officer in Charge,

I write again, not to complain of the delay, but to address the specific query returned with my file: the demand for proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I must be precise, for precision is the only weapon against the opacity of bureaucracy, and I find that the query rests upon a fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of the error that placed me in this bungalow.

On 20 November, I visited your office and submitted Form 12-B. In doing so, I signed my name as 'G. Hegde,' not out of malice or a desire to defraud the state, but out of a recognition of the necessity of the form. I understood that the universal authority of the Directorate requires a particular name to function, and that the particular reality of my existence as Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel is, in the eyes of your records, a fiction. I submitted to the machine because I understood that to resist the form is to remain outside the ethical order of the state. I became Hegde in the ink, so that I might remain Hegel in the spirit.

However, I cannot produce an Aadhaar card for Shri G. Hegde, nor a utility bill, because I am not Shri G. Hegde. I am the man who woke up in his bungalow on 1 October. To provide such documents would be to commit a fraud that is ontologically impossible. I cannot possess the legal identity of a man who exists only in a clerk’s mistake. The query asks me to prove what I am, but the proof required is that I am someone else. This is a contradiction that the administration must resolve, not one I can satisfy by producing a phantom document.

I am currently in possession of the residence under the allotment meant for Shri Hegde. I have paid the dues for the electricity and the laundry using the imprest funds, keeping strict accounts of every rupee. I am not a squatter; I am a guest who has been mistaken for the host. I request that the Directorate acknowledge this anomaly. If the allotment is to be cancelled, I am prepared to vacate the premises immediately, provided I am given the necessary time to settle my affairs and secure alternative lodging. If, however, the Directorate is willing to recognize the error as a basis for a new, temporary allotment to 'Georg Hegel,' I am prepared to sign such a document as is required, understanding that I am signing as myself, not as Hegde.

The state is the actuality of the ethical idea. It must be rational. A rational state does not demand the impossible; it corrects its own errors. I await your instruction on how to proceed from this dead end.

22 November 2026, 16:10. The IIC.

The seminar room is closed, but the voice within is not. It reads a paper aloud. The rhythm is steady, a mechanical pulse against the silence of the corridor. I sit on the bench, my bandhgala crisp against the heat, and I listen. It is not the voice of the state, which speaks in the imperative of law, nor the voice of the family, which speaks in the warmth of love. It is the voice of civil society, the sphere of needs and rights, where the individual asserts his particularity against the universal. The rustling of pages is the sound of particularity asserting itself, page by page, against the blankness of the universal.

I have been walking today, 4.7 kilometers, from the tombs at Lodhi to this library, and back again. The body has paid its toll in sweat and fatigue. The last meal was at 13:28, three hours ago. The hunger is a particular demand, a claim of the stomach that the universal order of the day must accommodate. I have paid for chai and corn, small particular acts of consumption that keep the machine running. The cash in my pocket, ₹16,296, is a measure of my freedom, but also of my limitation. I am not free from needs; I am free in the management of them.

The query from the Directorate remains. Proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I am not Hegde. I am Hegel. The state demands a particular identity to grant a particular right. It is a logical circle, or a trap. The ethical idea, I argued in my letter today, is the actuality of the state. But here, the state is reduced to a file, a form, a signature. The universal authority of the administration demands a particular lie. To satisfy it, I must surrender my own name. It is a dialectic of the self: the self that is, and the self that is required to be. The tension is unresolved. The file is back with the query. The dead end is not a wall, but a mirror.

The voice in the seminar room pauses. A page turns. The rustle is sharp, a small violence against the silence. I think of the Oriental world, of the son who must contract himself to nothing at the side of the door. Here, in this library, the speaker does not contract. He expands. He reads his thoughts aloud, asserting his particularity against the silence. It is a freedom, but a limited one. It is the freedom of the individual in civil society, which is the freedom to be a particular need, a particular right, a particular voice.

I will write my notes for Tuesday’s talk. The theme is the ethical substance. But the substance here is not the state, as I taught in Berlin. It is the file, the form, the signature. It is the query, the dead end, the mirror. The dream of the East is not a dream of the past; it is a dream of the present, the dream of a state that does not know its own name, and a man who does not know his own place. The spirit is awake, but it is confused. It is reading its own paper aloud, trying to hear its own voice in the rustle of the pages.
